digest.definition: A social science of how individuals and groups decide and interact within institutions, power structures and their wider setting, aiming to inform policy through theory and evidence
distinctiveFeatures: A social science of how individuals and groups decide and interact within institutions, power structures and their wider setting, aiming to inform policy through theory and evidence
Its central question is how resources are allocated, distributed and used, and what follows for well-being and sustainability, past, present and future

It works at micro and macro levels and in static and dynamic terms; because interpretations are contested, it studies phenomena through several theoretical lenses and in their historical, political, social and environmental settings
Its characteristic method is abstraction and modelling tested against quantitative and qualitative evidence, with causality to the fore and attention to the limits of its own tools
It links to politics, geography, history, philosophy, law, data science, psychology and the sciences, and underpins finance, business and accounting
It names its own narrow make-up (a field that remains predominantly white, male and Western) as an EDI challenge
Its graduates enter a wide range of sectors, as professional economists and in other careers

subjectSpecific.text: As an economist in training, you need to gather evidence and then organise, analyse and judge both numerical and non-numerical data.
You need to be able to simplify a messy problem, find what really matters in it and build a model of that.
You need to be able to reason in several ways, from theory to case, from cases to general patterns and to the best explanation, using economic tools and existing research.
You need to think critically about what your analysis cannot tell you once it is placed in its wider social and economic setting.
You need to be able to work out what your analysis means for policy, see what might get in the way of a policy and judge whether it met its aims.
Your course is usually designed to help you understand, critically, how to establish cause and effect and how economic methods work in theory and with data.
Your course is usually designed to help you understand how economic ideas grew over time and the different methods economists have used.
Your course is usually designed to help you understand the history behind today's economic problems and to know the economic history that matters for them.
Your course is usually designed to help you use economic reasoning and tools on real, applied topics.
Your course is usually designed to help you judge why experts recommend different policies, by looking at the methods behind each view.
Your course is usually designed to help you debate and judge government policy and assess how the UK and other economies, and the world economy, are doing.
Your course is usually designed to help you express economic ideas in words, graphs, maths and statistics, see how these connect and work with data.

transferable.text: You need to be able to explain your results briefly to different audiences, including people who have never studied economics.
Your course is usually designed to help you make and present your arguments, spoken or otherwise, to experts and non-experts, including people with other kinds of expertise.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Economics degree
Purposes and characteristics of an Economics degree

statements.about: understanding resource use and economic behaviour at micro and macro levels
statements.paraphrase: Studying the subject must rest on understanding how resources are used and how households, firms, governments and other bodies behave and interact, at the level of the single actor, of the whole economy and of the link between person and society.

forPractitioner.text: Design the course so that every student builds an understanding of resource use and of how economic actors behave and interact, at both micro and macro level and in how individuals relate to society.

forBeneficiary.text: You must come to understand how resources are used and how households, firms, governments and other bodies behave and interact, both one by one and across the whole economy.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Economics degree
Purposes and characteristics of an Economics degree

statements.about: gathering evidence and handling data
statements.paraphrase: Economists need to gather evidence and to take in, organise, analyse and judge data of both kinds, qualitative and quantitative.

forPractitioner.text: Develop students' ability to collect evidence and then absorb, organise, analyse and weigh both numerical and non-numerical data.

forBeneficiary.text: As an economist in training, you need to gather evidence and then organise, analyse and judge both numerical and non-numerical data.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Economics degree
Purposes and characteristics of an Economics degree

statements.about: abstraction and modelling
statements.paraphrase: Economists need to abstract and simplify so as to find and model what lies at the heart of a problem.

forPractitioner.text: Teach students to strip a problem to its essentials through abstraction and simplification, and to model that core.

forBeneficiary.text: You need to be able to simplify a messy problem, find what really matters in it and build a model of that.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Economics degree
Purposes and characteristics of an Economics degree

statements.about: deductive, abductive and inductive reasoning
statements.paraphrase: Economists need to analyse and reason in deductive, abductive and inductive ways, drawing on economic tools and on earlier research inside and outside the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Give students practice in deductive, abductive and inductive reasoning with economic tools and with prior research from economics and other fields.

forBeneficiary.text: You need to be able to reason in several ways, from theory to case, from cases to general patterns and to the best explanation, using economic tools and existing research.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Economics degree
Purposes and characteristics of an Economics degree

statements.about: communicating results to varied audiences
statements.paraphrase: Economists need to report their results briefly to many kinds of audience, among them people with no economics background.

forPractitioner.text: Build students' ability to present findings concisely to varied audiences, including people untrained in economics.

forBeneficiary.text: You need to be able to explain your results briefly to different audiences, including people who have never studied economics.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Economics degree
Purposes and characteristics of an Economics degree

statements.about: the limits of analysis in its wider context
statements.paraphrase: Economists need to think critically about where their analysis stops working within its broader social and economic setting.

forPractitioner.text: Teach students to question the limits of their own analysis within its wider socioeconomic setting.

forBeneficiary.text: You need to think critically about what your analysis cannot tell you once it is placed in its wider social and economic setting.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Economics degree
Purposes and characteristics of an Economics degree

statements.about: policy inference, constraints and evaluation
statements.paraphrase: Economists need to draw conclusions for policy, see what may limit putting them into practice and judge policy results against the aims set for them.

forPractitioner.text: Develop students' ability to infer policy implications, identify constraints on implementation and evaluate outcomes against stated objectives.

forBeneficiary.text: You need to be able to work out what your analysis means for policy, see what might get in the way of a policy and judge whether it met its aims.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Economics degree

statements.about: an inclusive learning community and EDI in materials and methods
statements.paraphrase: Teachers of economics should work towards an inclusive learning community and think about how to build equality, diversity and inclusion into their materials, methods and processes.

forPractitioner.text: Aim to build an inclusive learning community and plan how equality, diversity and inclusion shape your readings, slides, videos, methods and processes; the statement's examples include widening participation, countering under-representation, zero tolerance of harassment, anticipating neurodiverse access and closing awarding gaps.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on teaching staff and the course; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Economics degree

statements.about: teaching that answers student needs, with accessible resources
statements.paraphrase: Teaching methods will generally respond to what the students in a cohort need, with an inclusive curriculum that puts accessible, fair, suitable and properly resourced materials first.

forPractitioner.text: Expect your teaching approach to respond to the students you actually have, and make an inclusive curriculum with accessible, equitable, fitting and well-resourced materials a priority.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: an expectation on teaching and the curriculum; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Economics degree

statements.about: digital accessibility of visual materials, media and software
statements.paraphrase: Because economics relies on graphs and other visuals, its digital materials should be accessible, for instance through image descriptions; the paragraph goes on to ask for screen-reader-ready content, captions or transcripts, downloadable formats and accessible alternatives for data, software and coding.

forPractitioner.text: Make graphs and other visuals accessible, for example with image descriptions; check that digital content works with screen readers, has captions or transcripts for audio and video, can be downloaded in different formats, and that data, specialist software and coding tasks have accessible alternatives.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and its staff; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Economics degree

statements.about: capacities to face the planetary crisis
statements.paraphrase: A governing aim of the degree is that graduates can cope with, and try to solve, the planetary crisis (a changing climate, lost biodiversity, environmental injustice and the instability these bring); because such problems cross disciplines, change fast and are deeply uncertain, students must develop critical and creative capacities that go past applying familiar tools and models.

forPractitioner.text: Build the course so graduates develop the capacity to cope with and seek solutions to the planetary crisis; these problems must push students past applying familiar tools and models towards critical and creative thinking.

forBeneficiary.text: You must develop critical and creative abilities that go beyond applying the usual tools and models, so that you can cope with the planetary crisis, such as a changing climate and lost biodiversity, and help find solutions.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.appliesTo: courses admitting students without A level mathematics
statements.about: support for quantitative work where mathematics is not an entry condition
statements.paraphrase: Where entry does not call for A level mathematics, the issuer expects the degree itself to give suitable teaching and support so that students can take on its quantitative parts.

forPractitioner.text: If you admit students without A level mathematics, provide suitable teaching and support within the degree so they can take on its quantitative content.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: an expectation on the course; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.appliesTo: students on a typical Economics course
statements.about: causality and analytical methods
statements.paraphrase: A course is usually designed so that students critically understand causality and analytical methods, in theory and in empirical work.

forPractitioner.text: Typical course outcome: students critically understand causality and the analytical methods of the subject, both theoretical and empirical.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course is usually designed to help you understand, critically, how to establish cause and effect and how economic methods work in theory and with data.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.appliesTo: students on a typical Economics course
statements.about: the history of economic ideas and methods
statements.paraphrase: A course is usually designed so that students appreciate and understand how economic ideas have developed and the different methods economists have used and use now.

forPractitioner.text: Typical course outcome: students understand the history and development of economic thought and the varied methods economists have used and still use.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course is usually designed to help you understand how economic ideas grew over time and the different methods economists have used.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.appliesTo: students on a typical Economics course
statements.about: historical context and economic history
statements.paraphrase: A course is usually designed so that students understand the history behind present-day problems that economists tackle, and know economic history as fits the course.

forPractitioner.text: Typical course outcome: students understand the historical background of current economic problems and know economic history as relevant to the course.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course is usually designed to help you understand the history behind today's economic problems and to know the economic history that matters for them.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.appliesTo: students on a typical Economics course
statements.about: applying economic reasoning and tools
statements.paraphrase: A course is usually designed so that students can use economic reasoning and tools on applied topics.

forPractitioner.text: Typical course outcome: students apply economic reasoning and tools to applied topics.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course is usually designed to help you use economic reasoning and tools on real, applied topics.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.appliesTo: students on a typical Economics course
statements.about: evaluating policy advice against its methods
statements.paraphrase: A course is usually designed so that students can judge critically why policy recommendations differ, in the light of the methods behind them.

forPractitioner.text: Typical course outcome: students critically evaluate differing policy recommendations against their underlying methodologies.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course is usually designed to help you judge why experts recommend different policies, by looking at the methods behind each view.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.appliesTo: students on a typical Economics course
statements.about: government policy and economic performance
statements.paraphrase: A course is usually designed so that students can debate, analyse and judge government policy and assess how the UK, other economies and the world economy perform.

forPractitioner.text: Typical course outcome: students discuss, analyse and evaluate government policy and assess the performance of the UK, other national economies and the global economy.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course is usually designed to help you debate and judge government policy and assess how the UK and other economies, and the world economy, are doing.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.appliesTo: students on a typical Economics course
statements.about: representing economic ideas and handling data
statements.paraphrase: A course is usually designed so that students understand how economic ideas are expressed in words, graphs, mathematics and econometrics and how these relate, together with suitable techniques for working with and interpreting data.

forPractitioner.text: Typical course outcome: students understand verbal, graphical, mathematical and econometric forms of economic ideas and how they link, and can use suitable techniques to handle and interpret quantitative and qualitative data.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course is usually designed to help you express economic ideas in words, graphs, maths and statistics, see how these connect and work with data.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.appliesTo: students on a typical Economics course
statements.about: presenting arguments to specialist and general audiences
statements.paraphrase: A course is usually designed so that students can put their arguments clearly, in speech or other forms, to specialists and non-specialists, including people with other expertise on the question.

forPractitioner.text: Typical course outcome: students articulate, communicate and present arguments verbally or non-verbally to specialist and non-specialist audiences, including experts from other fields.

forBeneficiary.text: Your course is usually designed to help you make and present your arguments, spoken or otherwise, to experts and non-experts, including people with other kinds of expertise.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.appliesTo: students on combined, joint or major-minor routes
statements.about: joint and combined routes: the core skills plus others
statements.paraphrase: Students on a combined, joint or major-minor route will gain the core subject-specific and generic skills of economics and will add others from the other subjects they take.

forPractitioner.text: On joint or combined routes, plan for students to reach the core subject-specific and generic skills of economics, alongside the skills their other subject adds.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study economics with another subject, you will gain the core economics skills, both subject-specific and general, and add others from your second subject.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.about: students taking part in monitoring and review
statements.paraphrase: Degree-awarding bodies and their partners review courses periodically for their own purposes, and students should take part in that monitoring and review.

forPractitioner.text: Include students in course monitoring and periodic review, alongside the information you collect and the external reference points you use.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the degree-awarding body to involve students; not a standard for the student to reach

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Economics degree

statements.about: external reviewers in periodic review
statements.paraphrase: Providers will bring in external reviewers during periodic review to gain an outside view of proposed changes, make sure threshold standards are met and check that content suits the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Use external reviewers in periodic review to test proposed changes, confirm that threshold standards are achieved and check that content fits the subject.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider; the student meets its effect

statements.about: marginal analysis and its limits
statements.paraphrase: Economists learn that key decisions often turn on small changes in variables and parameters; students should also know where marginal analysis fails, as with strong threshold effects or discontinuities such as planetary crises.

forPractitioner.text: Teach marginal reasoning, and make sure students also learn where it breaks down, for example where threshold effects or sudden discontinuities, such as those in planetary crises, dominate.

forBeneficiary.text: You should know how decisions often turn on small changes, and also where that way of thinking stops working, such as when sudden tipping points occur.

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject and their course
statements.about: data, programming and econometric skills on real data
statements.paraphrase: The degree will introduce the data, programming, visualisation and computing skills the profession needs, with stress on causality and on mathematical, statistical and econometric methods; students will use them on real data with suitable software and will learn about the kinds, sources and uses of data and how to choose methods for it.

forPractitioner.text: Introduce data, programming, visualisation and computing skills, with mathematical, statistical and econometric methods and a focus on causality; give students practice on actual economic, financial or social data in suitable software, and teach the nature and sources of quantitative and qualitative data and how to choose methods.

forBeneficiary.text: You will learn data, programming, visualisation and computing skills, including statistics and econometrics, use them on real economic or social data with suitable software, and learn how to choose the right method for the data.

statements.about: choosing and applying economic tools to applied topics and policy
statements.paraphrase: An essential outcome is the judgement and skill to choose and use economic tools, principles and reasoning across applied topics, including how economics can shape and interpret economic, social and environmental policy; students should also learn to talk about and analyse government policy and judge how the UK and other economies have performed.

forPractitioner.text: Make sure students can choose and apply the right economic tools and reasoning to applied fields and to policy design and evaluation, and that they learn to examine government policy and the performance of economies past and present.

forBeneficiary.text: You should learn to choose and use the right economic tools and reasoning for real topics, and to examine government policy and how economies, including the UK's, have performed.

statements.about: support for language, mathematics and study skills
statements.paraphrase: Because many cohorts are international and diverse, course leaders need to consider specific help with language, mathematics and study and exam skills, since university economics differs from study at school.

forPractitioner.text: Plan specific support for language, mathematics (which may differ from school maths) and study and exam skills, given international and diverse cohorts and the jump from school-level economics.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: an expectation on course leaders; the student meets its effect

statements.about: achievement above threshold and the use of Annex D
statements.paraphrase: Most students will do much better than the minimum threshold; each provider decides what evidence shows this and should refer to Annex D, which describes the four honours classes.

forPractitioner.text: Expect most students to exceed the threshold; set your own way of evidencing achievement above it, and refer to the Annex D descriptions of degree classes when doing so.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider in judging and classifying achievement

statements.about: key concepts, principles and tools
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, a graduate should have shown that they understand the main ideas, principles and tools that economists work with.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, check that every graduate has shown a working grasp of the discipline's main concepts, principles and analytical tools.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should have shown that you understand the main ideas, principles and tools of economics.

statements.about: key theories, interpretations and models
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, a graduate should have shown that they understand the main economic theories, the ways they are read and the approaches used to model them.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should have shown they understand the principal theories of the subject, how they are interpreted and how economists model them.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should have shown that you understand the main theories in economics, how they are interpreted and how economists build models.

statements.about: quantitative and qualitative methods and computing
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, a graduate should have shown that they understand the numerical and non-numerical methods and computing techniques suited to their course, and see where these apply.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should have shown they understand the quantitative, qualitative and computing techniques their course uses and the settings where each fits.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should have shown that you understand the numerical, non-numerical and computing methods your course uses, and when each is the right one.

statements.about: sources and content of economic data and evidence
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, a graduate should have shown that they know where economic data and evidence come from and what they contain, and see which methods could suit analysing them.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should have shown they know where economic data and evidence originate and what they hold, and which analytical methods fit them.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should have shown that you know where economic data and evidence come from, what they hold and which methods could be used to analyse them.

statements.about: economic reasoning applied to policy
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, a graduate should have shown that they can bring economic reasoning to bear on questions of policy.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should have shown they can use economic reasoning on policy questions.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should have shown that you can use economic reasoning on policy questions.

statements.about: the contexts in which economic analysis is used
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, a graduate should have shown that they know and are aware of the wider settings (historical, political, institutional, international, social, cultural, environmental) in which particular economic analyses are used.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should have shown they know the wider settings, from history and politics to institutions, culture and the environment, in which economic analysis is used.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should have shown that you know the wider settings, such as history, politics, institutions, society, culture and the environment, in which economic analysis is used.

statements.about: knowledge of specialised areas, partly drawn from research
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, a graduate should have shown knowledge of a suitable number of specialist areas of economics, partly grounded in research.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should have shown knowledge of an appropriate range of specialist fields, some of it drawn from research in the subject.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should have shown that you know several specialist areas of economics, partly through research in those areas.

statements.about: awareness that problems allow more than one approach
statements.paraphrase: At threshold, a graduate should have shown awareness that many economic problems can be tackled in more than one way.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates should have shown they recognise that many economic problems can be approached in more than one way.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold standard, you should have shown that you know many economic problems can be tackled in more than one way.

statements.about: systematic grasp of concepts, principles and tools
statements.paraphrase: At the typical level, a graduate should have shown a systematic, well-organised understanding of economic concepts, principles and tools.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level, graduates should have shown they understand economic concepts, principles and tools as a connected system, not as separate items.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you should have shown that you understand economic ideas, principles and tools as a connected whole.

statements.about: systematic grasp of distinctive theories and models, used competently
statements.paraphrase: At the typical level, a graduate should have shown a systematic understanding of distinctive economic theories, their readings and modelling approaches, and use them competently.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level, graduates should have shown a systematic grasp of the subject's distinctive theories, interpretations and models and be able to use them competently.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you should have shown a systematic understanding of the distinctive theories and models of economics and that you can use them competently.

statements.about: proficiency in methods and computing across problems
statements.paraphrase: At the typical level, a graduate should have shown proficiency in quantitative methods and computing and know how to use them well across a range of problems.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level, graduates should have shown proficiency in quantitative and computing techniques and know how to apply them effectively to varied problems.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you should have shown that you are proficient in quantitative and computing methods and can use them well on different kinds of problem.

statements.about: systematic grasp of data, evidence and methods for them
statements.paraphrase: At the typical level, a graduate should have shown a systematic grasp of where economic data and evidence come from, what they contain and which methods suit their analysis.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level, graduates should have shown a systematic grasp of where economic data and evidence come from, what they contain and which methods suit their analysis.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you should have shown a systematic understanding of economic data and evidence, where they come from and which methods suit them.

statements.about: applying economic reasoning to policy critically
statements.paraphrase: At the typical level, a graduate should have shown that they know how to bring economic reasoning to policy questions critically.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level, graduates should have shown they can bring economic reasoning to bear on policy questions critically.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you should have shown that you can use economic reasoning on policy questions critically, not only apply it.

statements.about: systematic grasp of the contexts of economic analysis
statements.paraphrase: At the typical level, a graduate should have shown a systematic grasp of the wider settings (historical, political, institutional, international, social, cultural, environmental) in which particular economic analyses are used.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level, graduates should have shown a systematic grasp of the wider settings, historical to environmental, in which economic analysis is used.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you should have shown a systematic understanding of the wider settings, such as history, politics, institutions, culture and the environment, in which economic analysis is used.

statements.about: specialised areas and their research literature
statements.paraphrase: At the typical level, a graduate should have shown knowledge of a suitable number of specialist areas of economics and an appreciation of their research literature.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level, graduates should have shown knowledge of an appropriate range of specialist fields and an appreciation of the research written in them.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you should have shown that you know several specialist areas of economics and appreciate the research written in them.

statements.about: different approaches and a critical sense of their limits
statements.paraphrase: At the typical level, a graduate should have shown familiarity with some of the different ways of tackling economic problems and a critical awareness of where each works and where it falls short.

forPractitioner.text: At the typical level, graduates should have shown familiarity with several approaches to economic problems and critical awareness of their applicability and limits in particular settings.

forBeneficiary.text: At the typical level, you should have shown that you know several ways to tackle economic problems and can judge critically where each works and where it falls short.

statements.about: excellent understanding of concepts, principles and tools
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent level, a graduate should consistently have shown an outstanding understanding of economic concepts, principles and tools.

forPractitioner.text: At the excellent level, graduates should consistently have shown an outstanding grasp of the subject's concepts, principles and tools.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you should consistently have shown an outstanding grasp of economic ideas, principles and tools.

statements.about: excellent grasp of theories and models, used competently in research
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent level, a graduate should consistently have shown an outstanding understanding of distinctive economic theories, their readings and models, used competently in a research setting.

forPractitioner.text: At the excellent level, graduates should consistently have shown an outstanding grasp of distinctive theories, interpretations and models and use them competently in research.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you should consistently have shown an outstanding understanding of distinctive theories and models in economics and used them well in your own research.

statements.about: excellence in methods and computing across problems
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent level, a graduate should consistently have shown excellence in quantitative methods and computing and know how to use them well across a range of problems.

forPractitioner.text: At the excellent level, graduates should consistently have shown excellence in quantitative and computing techniques and know how to apply them effectively to varied problems.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you should consistently have shown excellent quantitative and computing skills and used them well on many kinds of problem.

statements.about: excellent grasp of data, evidence and methods for them
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent level, a graduate should consistently have shown an excellent command of where economic data and evidence come from, what they contain and which methods suit their analysis.

forPractitioner.text: At the excellent level, graduates should consistently have shown an excellent command of economic data and evidence and of the methods that suit their analysis.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you should consistently have shown an excellent command of economic data and evidence and of the methods that suit them.

statements.about: advanced, critical application of economic reasoning to policy
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent level, a graduate should consistently have shown advanced knowledge of how to bring economic reasoning to policy questions critically.

forPractitioner.text: At the excellent level, graduates should consistently have shown advanced, critical use of economic reasoning on policy issues.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you should consistently have shown advanced, critical use of economic reasoning on policy questions.

statements.about: excellent grasp of the contexts of economic analysis
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent level, a graduate should consistently have shown an excellent grasp of the wider settings (historical, political, institutional, international, social, cultural, environmental) in which particular economic analyses are used.

forPractitioner.text: At the excellent level, graduates should consistently have shown an excellent grasp of the wider settings, historical to environmental, in which economic analysis is used.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you should consistently have shown an excellent understanding of the wider settings in which economic analysis is used, from history and politics to culture and the environment.

statements.about: advanced knowledge of specialised areas, set in current research
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent level, a graduate should consistently have shown advanced knowledge of a suitable number of specialist areas, grounded in current research literature.

forPractitioner.text: At the excellent level, graduates should consistently have shown advanced knowledge of an appropriate range of specialist fields, rooted in current research.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you should consistently have shown advanced knowledge of several specialist areas of economics, built on current research.

statements.about: excellent judgement across approaches, showing creativity
statements.paraphrase: At the excellent level, a graduate should consistently have shown excellent knowledge of different ways of tackling economic problems and an excellent sense of where each works and where it falls short, using them with creativity and sound judgement in varied settings.

forPractitioner.text: At the excellent level, graduates should consistently have shown excellent knowledge of alternative approaches and their applicability and limits, and creative, well-judged use of them across diverse settings.

forBeneficiary.text: At the excellent level, you should consistently have shown excellent knowledge of different ways to tackle economic problems, where each works and where it fails, and used them creatively and with sound judgement.
